title: Soil mid-infrared spectroscopy
text: This course takes soil mid-infrared spectroscopy and rebuilds it inside R’s tidyverse and tidymodels. You’ll load real spectrometer output and engineer features from it. Then you’ll catch bad samples, fit and score a model, and run the same pipeline on a public global spectral library.

title: Soil mid-infrared spectroscopy
text:
Why tidyverse and tidymodels
Soil MIR spectroscopy already has capable, purpose-built R packages: prospectr and resemble, among others, cover preprocessing and spectral similarity in real depth. This course proposes an alternative: wrap that domain-specific work inside the tidyverse and tidymodels, the general frameworks most R users already know.
For me, four things make tidyverse and tidymodels worth building this course on.

The abstractions read naturally. recipe(), mutate(), step_snv(), each one names what it does. That keeps your attention on the domain instead of on R itself while modelling. Knowing what’s underneath still matters. This course spends real time unpacking it. But during modelling, the abstractions keep your attention on the pipeline rather than the implementation.
tidymodels also provides a harness for modelling and validating rigorously: splitting, resampling, tuning, and evaluation all follow the same structure, one that’s easy to get wrong by hand. A pipeline built this way is reproducible and repeatable.
Build it once, reuse it again and again, on a new dataset, a new target, a colleague’s laptop.
And building on tidyverse and tidymodels means building on a vast, expressive, mainstream ecosystem, one this course borrows rather than reinvents.

Base recipes ships no steps for spectra. This course adds a handful, wrapping prospectr and resemble underneath. Feature engineering tells that story properly. Everything downstream of them is standard tidymodels. We won’t reteach the tidyverse’s own documentation, its books, or its cheatsheets. Where this course points at a reference instead of re-explaining it, follow the link. That reference will outlast this course.

title: Soil mid-infrared spectroscopy
text:
How this course teaches
Each page runs top-down. It opens with the full step at the level you’d actually use day to day, one function call that returns a fitted model and a table of results. Only then does it open up to show what’s inside. The course runs the same way: The full pipeline assembles the whole thing once, then every page after it opens up one piece.
That’s deliberate. R functions like recipe(), mutate(), and tune() name what they do closely enough that someone with limited R experience can run the pipeline and follow its logic, even before they could write any of it themselves. Only later does peeling back a layer become worth the time. Every page that unpacks a function names its source file. Digging further is always one open file and the R console away.
R for Data Science covers the R foundations this course assumes, or skips past to keep moving. The Posit cheatsheets cover most packages this course uses, in a page or two each. If you want to understand R as a language, not just this pipeline, start with the Foundations section of Advanced R. Finally, the Tidy Modeling with R book proposes a deep dive into the Tidymodels framework.

title: Soil mid-infrared spectroscopy
text:
The course

Getting set up: install R, Positron, and the packages this course uses.
The full pipeline: load, preprocess, tune, test, and predict, once, end to end, before any of it gets explained.
Loading spectral data: read a folder of OPUS files and a wet chemistry CSV into one tibble.
Exploratory data analysis: look at the spectra and the soil properties before modelling anything.
Feature engineering: build a recipes pipeline out of resampling, SNV, and Savitzky-Golay steps.
Outlier detection: use PCA on the preprocessed spectra to find samples a model shouldn’t trust.
Evaluating performance: split the data, fit a model, and score it with tidymodels.
Preparing a model for inference: save a fitted model, load it again, and predict new spectra.
Preparing OSSL: pull a working sample from the Open Soil Spectral Library.
Predicting exchangeable potassium using OSSL: the same pipeline, run end to end on a public, global dataset.

title: Predicting Exchangeable Potassium using OSSL
text:
This page runs the pipeline from the earlier pages on the OSSL working sample built in Preparing OSSL: 4,548 soils with exchangeable potassium (Kex) and a MIR spectrum. It fits two models and compares them on the same test set. The first is PLS regression, as on the earlier pages. The second is Cubist, a rule-based model. The OSSL team found Cubist to be the best of the algorithms they tested (Safanelli et al., 2025).
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(plsmod)
library(rules)
library(hexbin)
source(here("R", "steps.R"))
source(here("R", "config.R"))
theme_set(theme_bw())
tidymodels_prefer()
SRC_FILE = here("data/ossl_mir_k_sample.rds")
TARGET <- "kex"

Splitting the data
With 4,548 samples, one validation set replaces cross-validation. initial_validation_split() splits the data three ways: 70% for training, 20% for validation and the remaining 10% for testing. That gives 3,183, 910 and 455 samples. Each candidate model is fitted on the training set and scored on the validation set. The test set is used once, at the end, as in Evaluating performance.
A validation set of 910 samples gives a stable score on its own. Cross-validation would fit every candidate 5 or 10 times. That costs much more time for little gain at this size.
With one validation set there is only one score per candidate. std_err is therefore NA, and select_by_one_std_err() cannot be used.

split <- initial_validation_split(data, prop = c(0.7, 0.2))

text:
Plotting predictions
Both models end with the same plot of observed against predicted values, so a small function draws it. With 455 test samples, single points overlap. geom_hex() counts the samples in each hexagon instead, and the fill colour shows the count on a log scale. Both axes are in log10 units, because step_log() transformed the outcome.

plot_obs_pred <- function(res, title = NULL) {
  collect_predictions(res) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = .data[[TARGET]], y = .pred)) +
    geom_hex(bins = 30) +
    geom_abline(lty = 2, colour = "grey30") +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, begin = 0.1, end = 0.85, transform = "log10") +
    labs(
      x = "Observed log10(Kex)", y = "Predicted log10(Kex)",
      fill = "Samples", title = title) +
    coord_obs_pred()
}

title: Predicting Exchangeable Potassium using OSSL
text:
Cubist

How Cubist works
Cubist builds a set of rules. Each rule is a condition on the predictors, for example “PC01 > 0.3 and PC04 ≤ -0.1”, and it holds its own linear regression. A sample is predicted by the linear models of the rules it meets. PLS fits one linear model to all samples. Cubist can fit different linear models to different kinds of soil.
Two settings change how the final prediction is made:

committees builds a sequence of Cubist models. Each new model is fitted to an outcome adjusted for the errors of the model before it, in a way similar to boosting. The prediction is the average over all committee members. committees = 1 is a single model.
neighbors adjusts each prediction using the most similar training samples. Cubist finds the neighbors nearest training samples and corrects the model prediction by how far the model was wrong on them. neighbors = 0 turns this off. The maximum is 9.



Using PCA scores as predictors
Cubist searches for rule conditions one predictor at a time. With about 1,700 highly correlated wavenumbers, that search is slow, and the rules pick individual wavenumbers that happen to fit the noise. step_pca() first compresses the spectra into a few principal components. threshold = 0.99 keeps as many components as it takes to explain 99% of the variance of the preprocessed spectra. tune_grid() fits the PCA inside the workflow, on the training set only.

rec_pca <- rec |>
  step_pca(all_predictors(), threshold = 0.99)

The number of components this keeps on the training set:

rec_pca |>
  prep(training = training(split)) |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  select(starts_with("PC")) |>
  ncol()

[1] 36




Tuning committees and neighbors
cubist_rules() comes from the rules package, which adds rule-based models to parsnip. The grid crosses 4 values of committees with every value of neighbors. That is 40 candidates, but neighbors does not change the fitted model, only the prediction. tune_grid() therefore fits only 4 models and scores the 10 neighbors values from each one. max_rules stays at its default: no limit.

cub_spec <- cubist_rules(committees = tune(), neighbors = tune()) |>
  set_engine("Cubist")


cub_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec_pca) |>
  add_model(cub_spec)


cub_grid <- crossing(
  committees = c(1, 10, 50, 100),
  neighbors  = 0:9
)


cub_res <- tune_grid(
  cub_wf,
  resamples = validation_set(split),
  grid = cub_grid
)

title: Predicting Exchangeable Potassium using OSSL
text:
Comparing the two models
Both models were tuned on the same validation set and tested on the same 455 test samples. Their test scores compare directly.

bind_rows(
  PLS    = collect_metrics(pls_final),
  Cubist = collect_metrics(cub_final),
  .id = "model"
) |>
  select(model, .metric, .estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = .estimate)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  model   rmse   rsq
  <chr>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 PLS    0.251 0.587
2 Cubist 0.251 0.585


On this sample, the two models score about the same. The difference is too small to mean anything. Another random split would change both scores by more than that.

How much data does a model need?
Figure 1 shows why. It comes from Albinet et al. (2022), who predicted Kex from KSSL MIR spectra with PLS and with a convolutional neural network (CNN). Both models were trained on growing subsets of the data. Each point is the mean R² over 20 different test splits, and the shaded band is ±1 standard deviation.






Figure 1: Learning curves of PLSR and CNN models predicting Kex in a growing data regime, using all Soil Taxonomy Orders. Mean and standard deviation of R² over 20 test splits. Reproduced from Albinet et al. (2022), Fig. 3, under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.



Three things stand out:

At about 4,500 samples, the size of this working sample, the CNN gains only about 0.05 in R² over PLS. The two bands overlap.
At that size, R² varies by about ±0.05 from one test split to another. A single split, as on this page, cannot separate two models that differ by less than that.
PLS levels off at about 0.64 from 10,000 samples. The CNN keeps improving, to about 0.77. The spectra hold more information about Kex than a linear model can use, but a flexible model needs a lot of data to find it.

Cubist is also a flexible model: each rule fits its own linear model to a different group of soils. Whether it follows the CNN curve or the PLS curve as the data grows is an open question, and one you can test.


Trying with more data
The working sample keeps 10% of the OSSL samples that have both a Kex value and a MIR spectrum. To use more:

In Preparing OSSL, raise prop in slice_sample(), or remove that line to keep all of them, about 45,000 samples.
Run that page again to save the larger sample. It overwrites data/ossl_mir_k_sample.rds.
Run this page again. Fitting takes longer as the data grows, especially for Cubist with many committees.

To compare models fairly, repeat the comparison over several random splits, or use cross-validation as in Evaluating performance. Then compare the spread of the scores, not only their means. That is how Figure 1 was built.

The pages before this one fit models and score them. Every sample they use has a lab value. Inference is what comes next: predicting a soil property from a new spectrum, with no lab value. This page takes the 7-component model chosen in Evaluating performance and prepares it for that job. It then saves the model to a file, loads it again as a new R session would, and predicts a few new samples.

title: Preparing a model for inference

An inference-ready workflow

data_log <- data |> mutate(across(all_of(TARGET), log10))
split    <- kennard_stone_split(data_log, prop = 50/70, cols = starts_with("wn_"))

rec <- recipe(data_log) |>
  update_role(all_of(TARGET),    new_role = "outcome") |>
  update_role(all_of(spc_cols),  new_role = "predictor") |>
  update_role(all_of(meta_cols), new_role = "metadata") |>
  update_role_requirements("metadata", bake = FALSE) |>
  step_resample(grid = RESAMPLING_GRID) |>
  step_snv() |>
  step_sg(w = SG_W, p = SG_P, m = SG_M)

wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec) |>
  add_model(pls_spec)

kennard_stone_split() works on the spectra only, so the split is the same as before. last_fit() scores the test set in log10 units, as on page 6.

final_res <- last_fit(wf, split)
collect_metrics(final_res)

1 rmse    standard      0.0961 pre0_mod0_post0
2 rsq     standard      0.924  pre0_mod0_post0



Back to percent with a post-processor
The workflow predicts log10 values. Whoever uses the model wants carbon in percent. Leaving the back-transform to them means everyone must remember 10^.pred, and nobody must forget it.
A tailor does it inside the workflow. The tailor package is the tidymodels post-processor. A recipe changes the data before it reaches the model. A tailor changes the predictions after the model makes them. adjust_predictions_custom() applies any expression to the predictions, here 10^.pred.

to_percent <- tailor() |>
  adjust_predictions_custom(.pred = 10^.pred)

We add the tailor only to the copy of the workflow we save. The evaluation above stays in log10 units. During evaluation, the observed values are in log10, because we logged them in data_log. A tailor at that stage would compare predictions in percent with observed values in log10.

model <- wf |>
  add_tailor(to_percent) |>
  fit(training(split))

title: Preparing a model for inference
section: Is a new spectrum within the model’s range?
text:
Is a new spectrum within the model’s range?
A model only knows the kind of spectra it was trained on. For a spectrum unlike any of them, it still returns a number, but nothing supports that number. The prediction itself gives no warning. A separate check has to.
The check uses the method from Outlier detection. We run the training spectra through the fitted recipe and fit a PCA on the result, keeping the components that explain 99% of the variance. A new spectrum is projected onto those components, and we measure its scaled Mahalanobis distance from the centre of the training spectra. A new spectrum beyond the cutoff is unusual compared with the training set, and its prediction needs caution.
extract_recipe() returns the fitted recipe from the workflow. bake() applies it.

train_baked <- bake(extract_recipe(model), new_data = training(split)) |>
  select(starts_with("wn_"))

pca_full <- prcomp(train_baked, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
n_pc <- which(cumsum(pca_full$sdev^2) / sum(pca_full$sdev^2) >= 0.99)[1]
pca <- prcomp(train_baked, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE, rank. = n_pc)
n_pc

[1] 17


On Outlier detection, resemble::dissimilarity() computes the distance. It estimates the covariance from Xr and Xu together. That is fine there, because Xu is only the centre of the scores. Here, Xu would be the batch of new spectra. An unusual new spectrum would then change the covariance, its own distance and the distances of the other new spectra, and the result would depend on which spectra happen to arrive together. The covariance must come from the training spectra alone.
We therefore compute the same scaled distance in base R. PCA scores are uncorrelated, and the variance of each one is pca$sdev^2, estimated on the training spectra. The squared distance is the sum of the squared scores, each divided by its variance. As in resemble, we divide by the number of components before taking the square root.

scaled_distance <- function(pca, x) {
  scores <- predict(pca, x)
  sqrt(rowSums(sweep(scores^2, 2, pca$sdev[seq_len(ncol(scores))]^2, "/")) / ncol(scores))
}

The cutoff, OUTLIER_CUTOFF in R/config.R, is the one chosen by eye on Outlier detection. The distances of the training spectra show how it sits against the spectra the model knows.

train_dist <- scaled_distance(pca, train_baked)
summary(train_dist)

title: Preparing a model for inference
text:
Saving the model
The saved file holds everything a prediction needs: the fitted workflow, the PCA and the cutoff. saveRDS() writes any R object to a file.

inference_kit <- list(model = model, pca = pca, cutoff = OUTLIER_CUTOFF)

dir.create(dirname(MODEL_FILE), showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(inference_kit, MODEL_FILE)

title: Preparing a model for inference
section: Using the model in a new session
text:
Using the model in a new session
The chunk below is what a new R session runs. rm() first clears every object except new_files, the list of OPUS files to predict. Nothing else from this page can help. Only the libraries, the course scripts and the saved file remain.
R/steps.R is the one dependency that is easy to miss. The saved workflow stores the step_snv(), step_sg() and step_resample() steps, but not the code that runs them. That code lives in R/steps.R, so it must be sourced before predict(). Without it, prediction fails. Anyone you share the model with also needs that script. A package would remove this dependency, and is the right home for these steps in the long run.

rm(list = setdiff(ls(), "new_files"))

library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
source(here("R", "prepare_data.R"))
source(here("R", "steps.R"))

kit <- readRDS(here("models", "carbon_pls.rds"))

predict_carbon() predicts each new spectrum and checks its distance in one call.

predict_carbon <- function(kit, spectra) {
  baked  <- bake(extract_recipe(kit$model), new_data = spectra) |>
    select(starts_with("wn_"))
  scores <- predict(kit$pca, baked)
  dist   <- sqrt(rowSums(sweep(scores^2, 2, kit$pca$sdev[seq_len(ncol(scores))]^2, "/")) / ncol(scores))

  spectra |>
    select(smp_id) |>
    bind_cols(predict(kit$model, spectra)) |>
    mutate(distance = dist, in_range = dist <= kit$cutoff)
}

section: Before using a model for real
text:
Before using a model for real

Refit on all samples. The model above learnt from the 48 training samples, so that the test score stays meaningful. Once you trust the test score, refit the same workflow on all the samples. More data usually gives a better model.
Measure new samples the same way. The model assumes the same instrument, sample preparation and number of replicate scans as the training set. The range check catches large differences, not all of them.
Keep the package versions. A saved workflow is safest with the package versions that fitted it. renv.lock records them.

threshold = 0.99 keeps as many components as needed to explain 99% of the variance of the preprocessed spectra. This is the rule used by Wadoux et al. Mahalanobis distance in feature space
The 2D checks above use only PC01 and PC02, and treat both axes as if they had the same spread. Mahalanobis distance from the centre of the scores uses all retained components and scales each one by its own variance.
We compute it with resemble::dissimilarity() and diss_mahalanobis(), as in Wadoux et al. (2021). Xr holds the scores of all samples. Xu holds the point to measure from, here the centre of the scores.

pc_cols <- names(scores)[startsWith(names(scores), "PC")]
X <- scores |> select(all_of(pc_cols)) |> as.matrix()

scores <- scores |>
  mutate(dist_feat = as.vector(resemble::dissimilarity(
    Xr = X,
    Xu = t(colMeans(X)),
    diss_method = resemble::diss_mahalanobis(center = FALSE, scale = FALSE)
  )$dissimilarity))

resemble divides the squared distance by the number of components before taking the square root. Each component adds about one unit to the squared distance of a typical sample. Without the division, distances grow with the number of components, and a value means something different for every dataset and every preprocessing. After the division, a typical sample sits near 1, however many components the 99% rule keeps. This also puts our values on the same scale as resemble and Wadoux et al. (2021).


Choosing a cutoff
There is no correct cutoff. We look at the distances, choose a value that separates the samples that stand out, and then check those samples one by one. The histogram shows the overall shape. The ranked list shows where the gaps are.

The rule of thumb in Wadoux et al. (2021) flags samples above 3. It suits large datasets. With few samples, the scaled distance has a ceiling: a sample that helped estimate the centre and the covariance cannot exceed \(\sqrt{(n-1)^2 / (n\,p)}\), with \(n\) samples and \(p\) components. Here that is 2, so a cutoff of 3 could never flag anything.
We set the cutoff by eye. RT_44 and RT_42 are at about 2.0, the ceiling itself. The next sample, RT_39, is at about 1.75. We put the cutoff in that gap, at 1.9, and record it as OUTLIER_CUTOFF in R/config.R. Preparing a model for inference uses the same value. Feature-space vs. target-space distance
Plotting one distance against the other splits the samples into four regions:

Both ordinary: nothing to discuss.
Unusual spectrum, ordinary chemistry: the spectrum is unusual but the reported properties look normal. This can be a matrix effect (particle size, moisture, packing) or an instrument artefact.
Unusual spectrum and chemistry: the spectrum and the chemistry agree that the sample is unusual. This is more likely a genuine rare soil than a measurement problem.
Ordinary spectrum, extreme chemistry: the spectrum looks like the others, but a reported property is extreme. Be most suspicious of these. A genuinely unusual composition usually leaves a trace in the spectrum, so a wet-chemistry or transcription error is more likely.

soil_long |> 
  ggplot(aes(sample = value)) +
  stat_qq(na.rm = TRUE) +
  stat_qq_line(na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~soil_prop, scales = "free")








carbon_org_perc and carbon_tot_perc curve furthest from the line, the same properties Loading spectral data flagged potassium_cmolkg for, only more so. Log-transforming pulls most of them back toward it:

soil_long |> 
  filter(value > 0) |>
  mutate(log_value = log(value)) |>
  ggplot(aes(sample = log_value)) +
  stat_qq(na.rm = TRUE) +
  stat_qq_line(na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~soil_prop, scales = "free")








carbon_org_perc makes the clearest case. Its raw skewness is 6.4, against 2.3 for potassium_cmolkg. Log-transformed, that drops to 0.1. The range runs from 0.08% to 49%, a roughly 600-fold spread across 69 samples. Three reasons favor fitting a model on log10(carbon_org_perc) instead of the raw value.
A model fit on the raw scale can predict a negative carbon percentage. Back-transforming a log-scale prediction with 10^y never can.
Squared-error loss on the raw scale weighs every percentage point of error the same, wherever it falls on the scale. That lets the handful of high-carbon samples dominate the loss, since their absolute errors are bigger. On the log scale, the same absolute error costs more for a low-carbon sample than a high one. The model can’t just chase the few high values at the expense of everyone else.
Skewed variables like this one also tend to have variance that grows with the value. Most classical inference tools assume that variance stays constant across the range. The log transform tends to even it out.
There’s a cost too. Coefficients and metrics like RMSE come back in log units, not percent carbon. Reading them in the original units takes a deliberate back-transform.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Soil properties correlation
Organic carbon and phosphorus correlate on the log scale: r = 0.40 (p = 0.018, n = 34, using only samples with both measured). It isn’t a tight relationship. Soils richer in organic matter tend to hold more phosphorus too.

data |>
  filter(carbon_org_perc > 0, phosporus_mgkg > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = carbon_org_perc,
    y = phosporus_mgkg
  )) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Organic carbon (%)",
    y = "Phosphorus (mg/kg)"
  )

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Spectra

All spectra

data |> plot_spectra()










Unpacking plot_spectra()
plot_spectra() reshapes the wavenumber columns into long format, then builds the plot below in stages. Colouring every one of the 70 samples by ID, the first attempt, produces a legend nobody can read:

spectra <- data |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wn_"),
    names_to = "wavenumber",
    names_prefix = "wn_",
    names_transform = list(wavenumber = as.numeric),
    values_to = "absorbance"
  )


ggplot(spectra, aes(wavenumber, absorbance, group = smp_id, colour = smp_id)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  labs(
    x = "Wavenumber",
    y = "Absorbance",
    colour = "Sample"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Dropping the per-sample colour and blending lines with alpha instead makes the overall shape visible:

ggplot(spectra, aes(wavenumber, absorbance, group = smp_id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, colour = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  theme_bw()








Tidying the axis breaks and labels gets to what plot_spectra() actually returns:

ggplot(spectra, aes(wavenumber, absorbance, group = smp_id)) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.35, colour = "steelblue") +
    scale_x_reverse(
        breaks = seq(500, 4000, by = 250),
        minor_breaks = seq(500, 4000, by = 125)) +
    labs(
        x = "Wavenumber (cm-1)",
        y = "Absorbance",
        colour = "Sample") +
    theme_bw()










Grouping by organic carbon quartile
Does carbon change how a spectrum looks? Colouring 70 overlapping lines by carbon content is hard to read, whatever the colour scale. Splitting the samples into four quartiles of organic carbon gives groups of about 17 soils each. ntile() assigns the quartile on the table of samples, one row per sample. On the long table of spectra, with one row per wavenumber, a sample at a quartile boundary could end up split between two groups. Each label gives the quartile’s range of organic carbon. RT_44, which has no carbon value, is left out.

carbon_quartiles <- data |>
  filter(!is.na(carbon_org_perc)) |>
  mutate(carbon_group = ntile(carbon_org_perc, 4)) |>
  group_by(carbon_group) |>
  mutate(carbon_range = sprintf(
    "Q%d: %s to %s%%",
    carbon_group, signif(min(carbon_org_perc), 2), signif(max(carbon_org_perc), 2)
  )) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(smp_id, carbon_range)

spectra_grouped <- spectra |>
  inner_join(carbon_quartiles, by = "smp_id")


ggplot(
  spectra_grouped,
  aes(wavenumber, absorbance, group = smp_id)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, colour = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ carbon_range) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  labs(
    x = "Wavenumber (cm-1)",
    y = "Absorbance",
    title = "Spectra grouped by organic carbon"
  )










Mean spectrum per quartile
The panels show the spread within each group, but not how the groups differ. Averaging the spectra of each quartile leaves one line per group.

p_means <- spectra_grouped |>
  group_by(carbon_range, wavenumber) |>
  summarise(absorbance = mean(absorbance), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(wavenumber, absorbance, colour = carbon_range)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_x_reverse(
    breaks = seq(500, 4000, by = 250),
    minor_breaks = seq(500, 4000, by = 125)
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "turbo", begin = 0.1, end = 0.9) +
  labs(
    x = "Wavenumber (cm-1)",
    y = "Mean absorbance",
    colour = "Organic carbon"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_means








The four means sit at about the same overall level, and not in carbon order. Mean absorbance across the whole spectrum correlates only weakly with log10 organic carbon: r = 0.24, p = 0.045. The clearer differences are local. Around 3620 to 3700 cm⁻¹, the lowest quartile has stronger peaks than the highest. This is where the O–H bonds of clay minerals absorb. Between about 2850 and 3000 cm⁻¹, where the C–H bonds of organic matter absorb, the difference is hard to see at this scale. The next section zooms in on it.


Zooming into the C–H band
At full width, the region where the C–H bonds of organic matter absorb is a small detail. coord_cartesian() zooms the view onto it. It crops what is shown without dropping any data. Setting axis limits with xlim(), or with limits in a scale, removes the points outside them before plotting instead. coord_cartesian() also crops only the axes it is given. With xlim alone, the y-axis would keep the range of the full spectrum, and the four lines would stay squeezed together, so ylim sets the y-range of the window too. Adding scale_x_reverse() to the saved plot replaces its axis breaks with finer ones.

p_means +
  scale_x_reverse(breaks = seq(2750, 3100, by = 50)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(3100, 2750), ylim = c(1.25, 1.9))








At this scale, the raw spectra show at most faint shoulders. Q3 and Q4 have small shoulders near 2920 and 2850 cm⁻¹, where the C–H bonds of organic matter absorb. Q1 and Q2 barely show them. The shoulders are small, about 0.05, and sit on a baseline that falls steeply across the window. Q3 and Q4 also show about the same shoulder, although Q4 holds far more carbon, and other compounds absorb in this window too. The raw spectra are consistent with a C–H signal, but they do not show it clearly. The sloping baseline hides it. Feature engineering takes the Savitzky-Golay first derivative of each spectrum, which removes slopes like this one and turns shoulders into clear peaks. That is one reason the pipeline preprocesses the spectra before modelling.

title: The full pipeline
text:
This page runs the whole pipeline once, start to finish: load spectra, preprocess them, tune and fit a model, test it, predict with it. Every step below gets its own full page later in the course. This page exists to show the shape of the whole thing before any of that detail.
The ring trial (RT) samples used throughout this course come from a real interlaboratory study: labs in several countries, including the IAEA’s, scanned the same soil samples on their own instruments, to see how much spectra disagree from lab to lab. Safanelli et al. (2023) covers what came out of it.

# --- Config ------------------------------------------------------------------
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(plsmod)
source(here("R", "prepare_data.R"))
source(here("R", "steps.R"))
source(here("R", "split.R"))
source(here("R", "config.R"))
tidymodels_prefer()

SPECTRA_DIR = here("data/RT_spectra")
SOIL_PROP_FILE = here("data/RT_wetchem_soildata.csv")
TARGET <- "carbon_tot_perc"

R/config.R holds the settings several pages share: EXCLUDED_SAMPLES, the preprocessing settings and the outlier cutoff. To try another setting, change it there and render the pages again.

# --- Loading ------------------------------------------------------------------
# EXCLUDED_SAMPLES dropped as known outliers -> 5-outlier-detection.qmd
data <- prepare_rt(SPECTRA_DIR, SOIL_PROP_FILE) |> filter(!smp_id %in% EXCLUDED_SAMPLES)


# --- Preprocessing --------------------------------------------------------------
# log-scale, resample, SNV, Savitzky-Golay -> 4-feature-engineering.qmd
spc_cols <- names(data)[startsWith(names(data), "wn_")]
meta_cols <- setdiff(names(data), c(TARGET, spc_cols))

rec <- recipe(data) |>
  update_role(all_of(TARGET), new_role = "outcome") |>
  update_role(all_of(spc_cols), new_role = "predictor") |>
  update_role(all_of(meta_cols), new_role = "metadata") |>
  step_log(all_outcomes(), base = 10) |>
  step_resample(grid = RESAMPLING_GRID) |>
  step_snv() |>
  step_sg(w = SG_W, p = SG_P, m = SG_M)

# --- Tuning -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# search num_comp, pick the best, lock it in -> 6-evaluating-performance.qmd
split <- kennard_stone_split(data, prop = 50/70, cols = starts_with("wn_"))
folds <- vfold_cv(training(split), v = 10, repeats = 10, strata = TARGET, breaks = 2)

wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec) |>
  add_model(pls(num_comp = tune()) |> set_engine("mixOmics") |> set_mode("regression"))

tune_res <- tune_grid(wf, resamples = folds, grid = tibble(num_comp = 2:20))
best <- select_best(tune_res, metric = "rmse")
final_wf <- wf |> finalize_workflow(best)

# --- Testing ------------------------------------------------------------------------
# fit on train, score once on the held-out test split
final_res <- final_wf |> last_fit(split)
collect_metrics(final_res) |> select(.metric, .estimate)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  .metric .estimate
  <chr>       <dbl>
1 rmse       0.0961
2 rsq        0.924 

# --- Predicting ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# .pred and TARGET are both log10 here -> 2-loading-data.qmd, 3-eda.qmd
collect_predictions(final_res) |> 
  select(all_of(TARGET), .pred) |>
  head()

  carbon_tot_perc  .pred
            <dbl>  <dbl>

2          0.332  0.329

4          0.318  0.320 
5          0.258  0.273

title: Getting set up
text:
Install the R packages
This project uses renv to pin exact package versions, the same idea as Python’s venv or conda. It gives you a project-local library instead of your regular R install. renv.lock records exactly what’s installed. Everyone in the course runs the same versions we tested against.

Open the project folder
Open the course folder itself, not a single file inside it:

Positron: File -> Open Folder…, then choose the course folder.
RStudio: double-click tidy-mirs.Rproj in the course folder, or use File -> Open Project… and choose it.

renv starts only when R starts inside the project folder, because the .Rprofile file in that folder activates it. The ZIP download includes this file, even though your file browser may hide it.


Let renv install itself
You do not need to install renv yourself. The first time R starts in the project folder, renv downloads and installs itself. When it is ready, the console shows a line like this:


Console

- Project '~/tidy-mirs' loaded. [renv 1.x.x]

renv may also say that some packages recorded in the lockfile are not installed. This is expected at this point. The next steps install them.
If you do not see the “Project loaded” line, check that you opened the folder and not a single file. Then restart R: in Positron, use the restart button in the Console panel; in RStudio, use Session -> Restart R.
This project was built with R 4.5.3. If your R version is different, renv shows a warning about it. You can ignore this warning: any recent 4.x release works.


Install the build tools
renv installs the exact package versions in renv.lock. When a version is no longer the current one on CRAN, CRAN has no ready-made binary for it, and renv compiles it from source. For this, your computer needs a compiler:

Windows: install Rtools, choosing the version that matches your R version.
macOS: install the Xcode Command Line Tools by running xcode-select --install in the Terminal. If a later build fails with an error that mentions gfortran, install it from the CRAN macOS tools page.
Linux: install your distribution’s R development package, for example r-base-dev on Debian and Ubuntu.

If you already have these tools, go to the next step.


Restore the packages
In the R console, run:


Console

renv::restore()

renv lists the packages it is going to install and asks Do you want to proceed? [Y/n]. Type Y and press Enter.
The first run downloads and installs everything listed in renv.lock into a project-local library. It can take a few minutes, longer if some packages compile from source. It touches nothing outside this project folder.


If renv fails
renv::restore() can fail behind a restrictive network proxy, on a locked-down institutional laptop, or in similar cases. If it does, install the same packages directly into your regular R library instead:


Console

install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("mixOmics")

install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse", "tidymodels", "here", "opusreader2",
  "skimr", "plsmod", "prospectr", "resemble", "hexbin", "glue",
  "rules", "Cubist"
))

Run the two parts in this order. mixOmics comes from Bioconductor, not CRAN, so install.packages() cannot find it. plsmod needs mixOmics, and cannot install until mixOmics is there.
This gets you everything you need for the course. It isn’t version-pinned. Let us know if something behaves differently from the demo.

Averaging replicate scans
Each sample was scanned four times. read_opus_tbl() keeps every scan as its own row. str_extract() pulls the shared sample ID out of each scan’s filename, for example RT_01 out of RT_01_001. Grouping by that ID and averaging every wavenumber column collapses the four scans into the one row per sample the rest of the pipeline needs.






Notedplyr, four verbs at a time



This chunk is your first look at dplyr, the package tidyverse uses for reshaping tables like this one. mutate() adds a column, group_by() marks rows to summarize together, summarize() collapses each group to one row, and across() applies the same function to several columns at once, here every column starting wn_. These four verbs cover most day-to-day data wrangling in R. The dplyr cheatsheet and the dplyr reference site cover the rest.



spectra_mean <- spectra |>
    mutate(smp_id = str_extract(spc_id, "RT_\\d+")) |>
    group_by(smp_id) |>
    summarize(across(starts_with("wn_"), mean))



Loading soil properties

title: Feature engineering
text:
Recipes
The full pipeline already built and used a recipe once, without explaining it. This page is that explanation. A recipe in tidymodels is a specification of preprocessing steps, written once and reused everywhere a model needs data in the same shape. The recipes package and the tidymodels recipes guide cover the general vocabulary this page assumes, alongside the Posit cheatsheets already pointed to from the course homepage.
Base recipes ships steps for the usual tabular preprocessing, centring, scaling, dummy variables, but nothing for a spectrum. step_snv(), step_sg(), and step_resample(), defined in R/steps.R, close that gap.
Each one wraps a prospectr or resemble function, prospectr::standardNormalVariate(), prospectr::savitzkyGolay(), prospectr::resample(), inside the contract a recipes step needs: a constructor, prep(), bake(), print(), tidy(). That’s what lets step_snv() sit in a recipe next to step_log() or any other tidymodels step. It gets ordered, tuned, and applied the same way every other step does.

Defining roles
Every column in data gets a role before any preprocessing happens: potassium_cmolkg as the outcome, the wn_* columns as predictors, everything else, sample_id, source, the other soil properties, as metadata. Metadata columns ride along through the whole recipe unchanged. They’re not used to fit anything, but having them still attached to data_processed later makes it possible to check whether prediction errors line up with, say, clay content or sample source, without a separate join back to the original data.

spc_cols <- names(data)[startsWith(names(data), "wn_")]
meta_cols <- setdiff(names(data), c(TARGET, spc_cols))

rec <- recipe(data) |>
  update_role(all_of(TARGET),  new_role = "outcome") |>
  update_role(all_of(spc_cols), new_role = "predictor") |>
  update_role(all_of(meta_cols), new_role = "metadata")

All steps together

  step_log(all_outcomes(), base = 10) |>
  step_resample(grid = RESAMPLING_GRID) |> 
  step_snv() |> 
  step_sg(w = SG_W, p = SG_P, m = SG_M)

title: Feature engineering
text:
Unpacking the recipe
The rest of this page adds one step at a time to rec. Each one’s effect on the spectra is visible on its own this way. Every version gets prep()ped then bake()d before plotting.
prep() is where a step learns anything it needs from the training data, a column’s mean and standard deviation for centring and scaling, say. bake() is where that learned information gets applied: to the training data here, to a validation or test set later, using the exact same numbers either time.
None of the three steps below actually estimate anything from the training set as a whole. SNV and Savitzky-Golay both act one row at a time, using only that row’s own values. Resampling only depends on the wavenumber grid, not on any sample’s measurements. prep() still runs before each one, mostly resolving which columns it applies to. The training/test separation it exists for matters most once a step needs to remember something computed across rows, a column mean for centring, say, rather than something computed within each row.

Resampling
This step does two things. step_log(all_outcomes(), base = 10) log-scales the outcome, the fix for potassium_cmolkg’s skew discussed back in Loading spectral data and Exploratory data analysis. step_resample() interpolates every spectrum onto RESAMPLING_GRID, an evenly spaced set of wavenumbers 5 cm⁻¹ apart, versus the roughly 2 cm⁻¹ spacing read_opus_tbl() returns. That cuts the predictor count from 1707 columns to 680. It also guarantees every sample lands on the same wavenumber axis, even where the source instrument didn’t.

rec_res <- rec |>
  step_log(all_outcomes(), base = 10) |>
  step_resample(grid = RESAMPLING_GRID)


rec_prep <- prep(rec_res, training = data, verbose = TRUE)

oper 1 step log [training] 
oper 2 step resample [training] 
The retained training set is ~ 0.45 Mb  in memory.

data_processed <- bake(
  rec_prep,
  new_data = NULL
)


data_processed |> plot_spectra()










SNV
step_snv() centres and scales each spectrum by its own mean and standard deviation, row by row, not column by column. That corrects for scatter effects, differences in particle size or packing that shift a whole spectrum up or down without changing its shape. Two spectra with the same underlying chemistry but different scatter come out looking the same after SNV. Two spectra with genuinely different chemistry stay different.

rec_snv <- rec |>
  step_log(all_outcomes(), base = 10) |>
  step_resample(grid = RESAMPLING_GRID) |>
  step_snv()


rec_prep <- prep(rec_snv, training = data, verbose = TRUE)

oper 1 step log [training] 
oper 2 step resample [training] 
oper 3 step snv [training] 
The retained training set is ~ 0.45 Mb  in memory.

data_processed <- bake(
  rec_prep,
  new_data = NULL
)


data_processed |> plot_spectra()










Savitzky-Golay
step_sg() fits a polynomial of order SG_P inside a moving window SG_W wavenumbers wide, centred on each point. It then reads off either a smoothed value or a derivative from that fit, depending on SG_M. With SG_M = 1 here, each spectrum gets its first derivative instead of a smoothed value. A first derivative removes baseline shifts entirely, rather than just correcting for them the way SNV does. It also tends to sharpen overlapping peaks.
Smoothing and differentiating both cost some data at the edges. prospectr::savitzkyGolay() trims (w - 1) / 2 wavenumbers off each end. That’s why the plotted spectrum below is narrower than the one above it.
SG_W = 15, SG_P = 3, and SG_M = 1 are sensible defaults here, tuned by eye on a dataset rather than picked arbitrarily. Does the Savitzky-Golay setting matter? compares them with other settings, as part of a model fit.

rec_sg <- rec |>
  step_log(all_outcomes(), base = 10) |>
  step_resample(grid = RESAMPLING_GRID) |> 
  step_snv() |> 
  step_sg(w = SG_W, p = SG_P, m = SG_M)

oper 2 step resample [training] 
oper 3 step snv [training]

  new_data = NULL

title: Evaluating performance
text:
Getting data
EXCLUDED_SAMPLES, RT_44 and RT_42, are left out. Outlier detection flags their spectra as the two most unusual. RT_44 has almost no lab data. RT_42 is not a measurement error. It is most likely an organic soil, such as a peat: its total and organic carbon are both 49%, and its pH is 3.3. A model cannot learn a soil type from a single sample, so leaving RT_42 out is a judgement about what the model can cover, not only a distance rule.

data <- prepare_rt(SPECTRA_DIR, SOIL_PROP_FILE) |> filter(!smp_id %in% EXCLUDED_SAMPLES)

title: Evaluating performance
text:
Splitting the data
The test set is set aside first. It stays untouched until the last step, last_fit(). Every decision before that, including the number of PLS components, uses the training set only. Otherwise the test score would be optimistic: the model would have been chosen partly because it did well on those same samples.
kennard_stone_split(), defined in R/split.R, chooses the training samples so that they cover the spectral space evenly. It works on PCA scores of the SNV-corrected spectra. It starts from the two most distant samples, then keeps adding the sample furthest from those already chosen. The test samples then fall inside the range the model has seen. initial_split() is the random alternative.

split <- kennard_stone_split(data, prop = 50/70, cols = starts_with("wn_"))

# or
# split <- initial_split(data, prop = 50/70)

title: Evaluating performance
text:
Cross-validation folds

What vfold_cv() does
The model has one setting to choose: the number of PLS components. Each candidate value needs a score on samples the model has not seen. The training set cannot give that score. Training error keeps falling as components are added, even after the extra components only fit noise. The test set cannot give it either, because it must stay untouched.
Cross-validation makes held-out data from the training set itself. vfold_cv() shuffles the 48 training samples and deals them into v = 10 groups, called folds, of 4 to 6 samples each. Each fold takes a turn as the assessment set. The model is fitted on the other 9 folds, 42 to 44 samples, and scored on the held-out fold. After 10 rounds, every training sample has been predicted once by a model that did not see it. The 10 fold scores are averaged into one estimate.
tune_grid() runs the whole workflow inside every fold, recipe included. The recipe is prepped on the 9 fitting folds only. Nothing learnt from the held-out fold leaks into the model.


Stratification
strata = all_of(TARGET) with breaks = 2 splits carbon_tot_perc at its median into a low half and a high half. Samples from each half are then dealt out evenly across the folds, so every fold gets a mix of low-carbon and high-carbon soils. Without this, a fold of 5 samples could hold only high-carbon soils by chance. Its score would then say more about that bad luck than about the model. Two bins is a coarse split. With only 4 to 6 samples per fold, a finer one would add little. The split uses the raw values, before step_log(). A median split gives the same two halves on either scale. all_of() tells vfold_cv() that TARGET holds a column name as a string. A bare strata = TARGET still works, but gives a deprecation warning.


Why repeat
A single 10-fold run depends on one random way of dealing the samples into folds. Shuffle again and the estimate changes. Each fold scores only 4 to 6 samples, so the RMSE of a single fold is very noisy. repeats = 10 runs the whole 10-fold procedure 10 times, each time with a new shuffle. That gives 100 fold scores per candidate instead of 10, and their mean is more stable.






NoteStandard error and the central limit theorem



Take \(n\) independent measurements, each with standard deviation \(\sigma\). Their mean has a standard deviation of \(\sigma / \sqrt{n}\). This is the standard error of the mean. The central limit theorem adds that the mean is approximately normally distributed as \(n\) grows, whatever the shape of the individual measurements. So the mean ± 2 standard errors gives a rough 95% range for the true value.
The gain follows a square root. 4 times more measurements halve the standard error. 100 fold scores instead of 10 cut it by \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2\).
collect_metrics() reports exactly this. Its std_err column is the standard deviation of the fold scores divided by \(\sqrt{n}\), with n = 100 here.




Why the gain is smaller than it looks
The \(\sigma / \sqrt{n}\) formula needs independent measurements. The 100 fold scores are not independent:

Within one repeat, any two fitting sets share 8 of their 9 folds, about 90% of their samples. The models they produce are very similar.
Across repeats, the same 48 samples are reshuffled. No new soil ever enters.

Repeating averages away the noise that comes from how the folds were dealt. It cannot remove the noise that comes from which 48 soils were collected. A different set of 48 soils from the same region would give a different curve. No amount of repeating on the current set shows that.
The effective number of independent measurements is therefore much smaller than 100, and std_err is too small. Read it as a lower bound on the real uncertainty. It is still useful to compare candidates with each other, because they all use the same folds. There is no simple fix. Bengio and Grandvalet (2004) show that no unbiased estimator of the variance of k-fold cross-validation exists.

set.seed(123)

folds <- vfold_cv(
  training(split),
  v = 10,
  repeats = 10,
  strata = all_of(TARGET),
  breaks = 2
)

Evaluating performance
text:
Tuning the number of components
The grid lists the candidate values: 2 to 20 components, 19 candidates.

num_comp_grid <- tibble(num_comp = 2:20)

tune_grid() fits the workflow for every candidate in every fold: 19 candidates × 100 folds, 1,900 fits. Each fit is scored on its held-out fold with the default regression metrics, RMSE and R².

tune_res <- tune_grid(
  wf,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = num_comp_grid
)

title: Evaluating performance
text:
Choosing the number of components
select_best() returns the candidate with the lowest mean RMSE.

best_rmse <- select_best(tune_res, metric = "rmse")
best_rmse

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  num_comp .config         
     <int> <chr>           
1        7 pre0_mod06_post0



The one-standard-error rule
select_best() treats the smallest mean as the winner, even when a simpler candidate scores almost the same. With PLS, fewer components means a simpler model. A simpler model is usually more stable on new samples, and less likely to have fitted quirks of the training set. The one-standard-error rule, from Breiman et al. (1984) and described in Hastie et al. (2009), makes that trade-off explicit. It picks the simplest candidate whose score is within one standard error of the best.
select_by_one_std_err(tune_res, metric = "rmse", num_comp) does this in 5 steps:

It keeps only the rmse rows of collect_metrics(tune_res).
It finds the candidate with the lowest mean RMSE. This is the one select_best() returns.
It computes a bound: the best mean plus the std_err of the best candidate. Only the standard error of the best candidate is used, not that of each candidate.
It keeps every candidate whose mean RMSE is at or below the bound. The best candidate always qualifies.
It sorts those candidates by the arguments passed after metric, here num_comp in ascending order, and returns the first row.

The last argument defines what “simplest” means. The function cannot guess it. For PLS, fewer components is simpler, so num_comp sorts in the right direction. For a penalised regression, a larger penalty is simpler, and the call would need desc(penalty) instead.
The rule inherits the weakness of std_err. That value is too small here, as explained above, so the bound is tight. The rule stays closer to select_best() than it would with a realistic standard error.

best_1se <- select_by_one_std_err(tune_res, metric = "rmse", num_comp)

title: Preparing OSSL
text:
The Open Soil Spectral Library
The RT dataset used so far has 70 samples. That is enough to learn the workflow, but not enough to build a model that works on soils from other places. The Open Soil Spectral Library (OSSL) is a much larger, public alternative.
OSSL is compiled by the Soil Spectroscopy for Global Good initiative. It brings together soil spectral libraries from many sources, including the USDA NRCS Kellogg Soil Survey Laboratory (KSSL), ICRAF-ISRIC, the Africa Soil Information Service (AfSIS) and LUCAS. It holds more than 135,000 entries, with MIR, VisNIR and NIR spectra and the matching wet chemistry. Each source used its own column names and units. OSSL maps them all onto one naming scheme, so the whole library can be used as one table. Safanelli et al. (2025) describe how it was built.

How OSSL is distributed
OSSL is distributed as static files in a public Google Cloud Storage bucket. The database access page lists them. There is one file for the whole library, or separate files for site data, lab data, MIR spectra and VisNIR spectra. Each comes as compressed CSV (.csv.gz) or as a qs file for R. The static files can only be downloaded whole. An experimental API allows filtered queries.
Each file comes at two levels:

Level 0 (L0) keeps each property as measured by its original analytical method.
Level 1 (L1) converts properties measured with different methods to a common reference method, using published transformation rules.

This page uses L0, so every Kex value below comes from the same laboratory method.


Column names
Every column name follows the pattern concept.method_unit_datatype, described on the database description page. For example:

id.layer_uuid_txt is the unique identifier of a soil layer, as text.
k.ext_usda.a725_cmolc.kg is extractable potassium, measured with USDA method A725, in cmol(+)/kg. Method A725 displaces exchangeable potassium with 1 M ammonium acetate at pH 7.0.
scan_mir.600_abs is the MIR absorbance, in log10 units, at 600 cm⁻¹. MIR columns run from 600 to 4000 cm⁻¹, every 2 cm⁻¹.

title: Preparing OSSL
text:
Why exchangeable potassium
This course uses exchangeable potassium (Kex) as its OSSL example because of its role after nuclear accidents. Caesium and potassium behave alike in soil and in plants. Plant roots take up radiocaesium through the same pathways as potassium. When a soil holds plenty of exchangeable potassium, crops take up less radiocaesium. Potassium fertilisation is therefore a standard countermeasure on contaminated farmland, as used after the Chernobyl and Fukushima accidents. Planning it well needs Kex values for many fields, quickly. Wet chemistry is too slow and too costly for that. MIR spectroscopy is fast and cheap once a calibration model exists.
Albinet et al. (2022) trained such models on about 40,000 KSSL MIR spectra with Kex measured by the same 1 M ammonium acetate method. A convolutional neural network raised R² from 0.64, for a PLS baseline, to 0.79. This course stays with PLS and a small subset of the data. It is a simple, complete example to build on.

title: Preparing OSSL
text:
Downloading the library
src points to the whole library at level 0, as one compressed CSV. dest is where the working sample will be saved, inside the course data/ folder.

src = "https://storage.googleapis.com/soilspec4gg-public/ossl_all_L0_v1.2.csv.gz"
dest = here("data", "ossl_mir_k_sample.rds")

read_csv() downloads and reads the file in one step. The file is large. This takes a while and needs plenty of memory. You only need to run this page once. Predicting exchangeable potassium using OSSL reads the small file saved at the end, not the full library.

data = read_csv(src)

title: Preparing OSSL
text:
Detection limit
A laboratory method cannot reliably measure values below its method detection limit (MDL). For Kex measured with 1 M ammonium acetate at pH 7, as in KSSL, the MDL is 0.06 cmol(+)/kg. Values close to it are uncertain, so samples below a threshold are dropped.
Albinet et al. (2022) set that threshold at 0.12 cmol(+)/kg, twice the MDL. It is low enough to keep 0.14 cmol(+)/kg in the data. In the Fukushima area, that Kex level kept the radiocaesium concentration of 99% of brown rice below the target level. The paper gives the full reasoning. kex_threshold holds this threshold.

# Kex threshold: 2 × MDL (MDL = 0.06 cmol(+)/kg)
kex_threshold <- 0.12 # cmol(+).kg−1

title: Preparing OSSL
Preparing OSSL
text:
Scaling up
The sample is deliberately small. To go further:

Change prop in slice_sample(), or remove the line, to use all of the roughly 45,000 samples that pass the filters.
Replace k.ext_usda.a725_cmolc.kg with another property, and set a detection level that suits its method.
Filter on dataset.code_ascii_txt to keep or compare particular source libraries.
Use the level 1 file to combine properties measured with different methods.

title: Does the Savitzky-Golay setting matter?
text:
The other pages fix the Savitzky-Golay (SG) parameters at w = 15, p = 3, m = 1. These are sensible defaults from practice, not values fitted to any dataset. This page checks whether the choice matters on the RT data. It compares a few contrasting SG settings, and a model without SG, with the same repeated cross-validation as Evaluating performance. Read that page first: this one reuses its split, its folds, and its one-standard-error bound, and does not explain them again.

Data, split, and folds

title: Does the Savitzky-Golay setting matter?
text:
What the three parameters do
SG fits a polynomial of degree p to the w points centred on each wavenumber. It then replaces that point with the fitted value (m = 0) or a derivative of the fitted polynomial (m = 1 or m = 2).

w, the window size, sets how much the spectrum is smoothed. A wider window averages away more noise, but it also flattens narrow absorption bands. w counts points on the resampled grid, not wavenumbers. Here the grid has one point every 5 cm⁻¹, so w = 7 spans 30 cm⁻¹ and w = 21 spans 100 cm⁻¹.
p, the polynomial degree, sets how closely the fit can follow the shape inside the window. A higher degree keeps sharper peaks, but smooths less.
m, the derivative order, sets what is read off the fit. m = 0 smooths only. m = 1 removes a constant baseline offset. m = 2 also removes a linear baseline slope. Each derivative also amplifies noise, which a wider window has to compensate for.

w must be odd, so that the window has a centre point. m must not exceed p.

title: Does the Savitzky-Golay setting matter?
text:
The settings compared
The settings below cross the three derivative orders with a narrow and a wide window. p = 2 is valid for all three derivative orders, so it stays fixed and only one thing changes at a time. The course default is added as a reference.

sg_settings <- tribble(
  ~w,  ~p, ~m,
   7L, 2L, 0L,
  21L, 2L, 0L,
   7L, 2L, 1L,
  21L, 2L, 1L,
   7L, 2L, 2L,
  21L, 2L, 2L,
  15L, 3L, 1L
)

title: Does the Savitzky-Golay setting matter?
Does the Savitzky-Golay setting matter?
text:
Results
The results of both searches go into one table, with a label for each setting.

rmse_res <- bind_rows(
  collect_metrics(res_base) |> mutate(setting = "no SG"),
  collect_metrics(res_sg)   |> mutate(setting = glue::glue("w={w}, p={p}, m={m}"))
) |>
  mutate(default = setting == glue::glue("w={SG_W}, p={SG_P}, m={SG_M}"))


RMSE against the number of components
Each line is one setting.

rmse_res |>

  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Number of PLS components", y = "RMSE (log10 units)", colour = NULL,
       title = "CV RMSE by preprocessing setting")










Best RMSE of each setting
For each setting, the table below keeps the number of components with the lowest mean RMSE. bound is the one-standard-error bound of the overall best: its mean RMSE plus its standard error.

  group_by(setting) |>
  slice_min(mean, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

best_row <- best_per_setting |> slice_min(mean, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
bound    <- best_row$mean + best_row$std_err

best_per_setting |>
  mutate(within_bound = mean <= bound) |>

  geom_vline(xintercept = bound, linetype = "22") +

spread_sg  <- diff(range(best_per_setting$mean))

3 of the 8 settings are inside the bound. Between the best and the worst setting, the lowest mean RMSE varies by 0.046. For the best setting alone, the RMSE varies by 0.12 across the number of components. On this dataset, the number of components matters more than the preprocessing setting.
The standard errors are also too small, as Evaluating performance explains: the 100 fold scores are not independent. The real uncertainty is wider than the error bars, so the settings are even harder to separate than the plot suggests.

title: Does the Savitzky-Golay setting matter?
text:
What this means in practice
With 48 training samples, the data cannot reliably separate most SG settings. The ranking is also unstable. Removing a single sample, RT_42, reordered most of the table and moved several settings across the bound. Three points still stand out:

Settings that amplify noise do worse. Each derivative amplifies noise, and a narrow window averages little of it away. The second derivative with w = 7, a window of 30 cm⁻¹, is clearly the worst setting.
Settings without a derivative do well here. Smoothing alone, or no SG at all, scores at or near the top. PLS combines hundreds of wavenumbers into each component, which already averages away much of the noise that SG smoothing would remove.
The course default is not among the best here. Its lowest mean RMSE is 0.146, against a bound of 0.139. The gap is small. One sample was enough to move the default from inside the bound to outside it, so this is weak evidence against the setting.

The choice of SG setting is therefore not worth a long search: avoid settings that amplify noise, and keep a standard one. The number of PLS components matters much more, and tuning it is essential.
The course keeps w = 15, p = 3, m = 1 as its default. The first derivative is a standard choice for MIR spectra: it removes baseline shifts, and Feature engineering shows what it does to a spectrum. To try another setting on every page, change SG_W, SG_P and SG_M in R/config.R and render the pages again. Compare settings with cross-validation results, as on this page, not with the test score. Choosing with the test set makes its score optimistic.
This holds for this dataset, not in general. Two things can change the answer:

More samples. With thousands of samples, like the OSSL sample, the error bars shrink. Differences between settings that are hidden here can become visible. The same check is then worth running, with a validation set instead of repeated cross-validation to keep the cost down.
The resolution of the spectral grid. w counts grid points. On a grid with one point every 10 cm⁻¹, w = 21 spans 200 cm⁻¹, not 100. A setting tuned on one grid does not carry over to another grid as it is.
